idiom_name: interceptor/decorator around the audited operation + dedicated audit sink
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: place an interceptor between caller and target that receives the invocation context (operation, arguments, caller identity), records an attempt event, delegates to the target and then records the outcome (success, failure, denied) under the same correlation id. Enrol auditable operations through a binding or registry so neither the target nor its callers change, and write every event to one sink with a fixed schema. The interceptor must be able to abort the delegation (for fail-closed policies), and calls that do not pass through the seam are not audited at all — so the seam has to be the only route to the target.
code_sketch:
on_invocation(op, args, caller):
    event = audit_event(actor=caller, action=op.name, target=op.owner, outcome="attempt")
    sink.write(event)
    try:
        result = op.delegate(args)
        sink.write(event.with_outcome("ok"))
        return result
    except Denied as e:
        sink.write(event.with_outcome("denied", reason=e.reason)); raise
    except Exception as e:
        sink.write(event.with_outcome("failed", reason=type(e).__name__)); raise
pitfalls: Record only the attempt -> the trail cannot distinguish a denial, failure or success -> write a terminal outcome under the same correlation id before propagating the result or exception.

Audit a convenient subset of sensitive methods -> self-invocation, raw references or an unbound operation bypass the seam silently -> verify bindings and force access through one gateway or an infrastructure-level audit.
Put the audit write in the business transaction -> rollback erases the evidence of the attempted action -> use a separate transaction or an outbox and monitor delivery explicitly.
Serialize raw arguments or return values -> credentials, tokens and personal data accumulate in the audit trail -> whitelist and redact fields before constructing the event.
Assume an asynchronous queue preserves order -> concurrent workers can drop or reorder events and break hash chains -> sequence at the sink and alert on gaps.
Lose the correlation id at a queue or background-job boundary -> investigators cannot join the request to its downstream actions -> propagate trace context explicitly.
Use wall-clock timestamps from unsynchronized hosts -> event chronology becomes misleading across services -> use UTC with synchronized clocks plus a monotonic or sink sequence.

Leave sink failure handling implicit -> availability and accountability trade-offs become an accidental fail-open or fail-closed policy -> declare the policy per operation and alert on write failures.

Treat the interceptor as authorization -> a bypassed or misbound interceptor permits the action while producing no record -> keep enforcement in a reference monitor and use the interceptor as detective control.
